newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir team readies for repairs after old crew leaves.
newsitem.headline: Mir team readies for repairs after old crew leaves.

text.p: The Russian-U.S. crew aboard the crippled Mir space station planned on Friday to step up preparations for making vital repairs after two cosmonauts returned safely to earth.

Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin were reunited with their families after landing in the steppes of Kazakhstan on Thursday and flying back to the Star City training centre outside Moscow.

Looking tired but well, they celebrated on their flight from the steppes with a feast of caviar and French red wine. They were then met by their wives with large bouquets of flowers and by colleagues with salt and bread, a traditional greeting.
He hoped he and Lazutkin would not be made scapegoats for Mir's recent woes but also said they were not heroes for what they had done.
"It's very easy to find someone to shoot, pop, pop, and he's gone. Who does this help?" he said during the return flight from Kazakhstan to Star City.

Mir suffered the worst accident in its history on June 25 when it collided with its cargo ship, damaging the power supply. Other problems included a fire on Mir in February and a stress-induced irregular heart beat suffered by Tsibliyev.
A Russian space official said the new crew on Mir had made progress by repairing the main Elektron oxygen generating system, but it had not yet been started up.

On Friday, the three men left on Mir -- commander Anatoly Solovyov, engineer Pavel Vinogradov and NASA physicist Michael Foale -- plan to get into their Soyuz capsule to redock it on the other side of the station.

"On Friday they will undock, go around the station to look at its construction and video it," Deputy Flight Director Igor Goncharov told Reuters. "They will dock at the other port near the Spektr module."

The Spektr module was punctured during the June accident, and is now airless, dark and sealed off from the rest of the station. The two Russian cosmonauts will open the hatch next Wednesday to reattach cables linked to Spektr's solar panels in a risky repair job intended to restore the ship's energy system.
"Any active operation is always dangerous. There is always the possibility of technical failure," Goncharov said. "But it's a necessary operation and the cosmonauts are prepared for this."
On Sunday, Mir will redock with its old Progress resupply ship, the procedure that caused the June accident. This time the crew expects to do the operation on automatic pilot.
Russian space agency doctors said that adjusting to earth may be more difficult for Tsibliyev than other returning cosmonauts because media have blamed him for the accident.
President Boris Yeltsin said last week "human factors" appeared to have caused the accident.

"Vasily feels responsible that he didn't fulfill his scientific programme because he had to do all that repair work," Goncharov said. "Yeltsin's words won't have the best psychological effects for either of the crew members."
